title: Skill Invocation and Routing
service: SkillRoute: a skill host's invocation layer: core and host-extension policy adapters, a router that serves one catalog snapshot (eligibility first, relevance second, abstain or ask), a re-entrant JSON run state, argument binding across the three representations, an NDJSON trace of skill lifecycle stages across a multi-turn session, and skill-to-skill calls on the host's own chain

parts.lesson_anchor: Eligibility must precede ranking (incident-triage 0.80 blocked, incident-review eligible); Human and model invocation form a 2x2 matrix (user-invocable: false and disable-model-invocation: true, and the confusing detail); Routing is classification with an abstain option; Exercise 4 (ambiguity margin); code/main.py route_request, ExtensionPolicyAdapter, _extension_false/_extension_true
planted_bugs: Router.route's implicit branch scores every skill, takes the best and only then asks the policy, so incident-triage (0.8, model invocation disabled) makes the whole request abstain and incident-review (0.5) is never considered

ExtensionPolicyAdapter.allows maps the host fields to the wrong actors: disable-model-invocation: true blocks every actor and user-invocable: false blocks the model; the test sees it one call up, in Router.route refusing a human's explicit incident-triage and in Router.eligible's human and model views
no ambiguity rule: the lesson code's max(key=(score, name)) lets the alphabetically last name win a tie, and InvocationPolicy.ambiguity_margin is never read
Router._catalog parses every frontmatter block again on every route and eligible call, O(catalog) per explicit invocation
parts.timing_assert: 50 explicit human invocations against a 3000-skill catalog, after one warm-up request and gc.collect(), under 0.02 s. Measured here at load average 5 to 6: the per-request reparse takes 0.27 to 0.32 s (at least 13x the limit, about 0.3 s per run), the fixed starter and the reference 0.06 to 0.09 ms (more than 200x under it); parsing once but scanning the list for the name takes about 0.7 ms, and an lru_cache around parse_frontmatter about 4 ms
parts.overfix_guard: host fields written as text (quoted "false", unquoted False, TRUE) must mean what the booleans mean, which catches flags precomputed with bool(), case-sensitive comparisons and boolean-only checks; the core adapter still gives host fields no meaning; the application channel still reaches a skill neither humans nor the model may invoke; naming a skill still goes through the policy; only eligible skills make a request ambiguous; a tie below the threshold abstains instead of asking
traps: max() over an empty eligible list, or a fallback to the best blocked skill
user-invocable: false also blocking the model, disable-model-invocation applied to every actor or to the model but not to agents, host fields closing the application channel

ties broken by name in either direction, the margin compared with <, exact ties only, ambiguity judged over blocked skills, candidates without the best skill or in score order, an ambiguous request still activating
the catalog parsed again for every request

parts.lesson_anchor: The five invocation stages (eligible, selected, activated, executing, completed; a trace that records only skill_used=true hides the boundary); Context lifecycle is host-specific (a body may remain, be summarized during compaction, or run elsewhere; tool allowances may last one turn while instructions persist longer; state what must be reloaded)

parts.lesson_anchor: Skill-to-skill invocation is a tool-like edge (target_skill, a bounded task and artifact paths, the expected response contract, the reason, a fallback if unavailable, a maximum depth or cycle rule; the host decides whether it shares context or runs in a fork); Exercise 5 (maximum composition depth and a two-skill cycle); Use It (missing_dependency: stop); quiz Q12 (a host-recorded chain instead of self-reported caller and depth)

deviations: Part 1: the router is an object that serves one catalog snapshot and takes the SKILL.md frontmatter blocks discovery found, parsed by a given parser that follows lesson 22's portable field table. The planted performance bug is Router._catalog reparsing the whole catalog on every request, and the timing uses 50 explicit invocations against 3000 skills instead of 2000 skills times 50 implicit requests: implicit routing has to score every eligible skill on every request, and measured here reparsing costs about 2.5 microseconds per skill against 1 to 1.5 for scoring, so a fixed version can only be about 10x faster there, short of the 8x margin on both sides. Explicit invocations make the fix O(1) per request, as identity-first invocation should be.

Part 1: the overfix guard writes the host fields as frontmatter text (quoted "false", unquoted False and TRUE), because the given parser keeps every value except unquoted lowercase true/false as text; bool(value) then turns "false" into True. Ambiguity is an abstention that lists the tied skills in a candidates field, with InvocationPolicy.ambiguity_margin from Exercise 4; the threshold is checked before ambiguity.

Part 2: no simulated crash in the middle of a write. Chapter 13 already tests that trap in 04 and 13, and a trap class may appear at most twice per chapter; the reference still writes a temporary file and os.replace, and the interviewer asks about it. The stale in-memory copy (13 and 15) is left out for the same reason: every resume reads the file. In their place: the full commit id (a moved tag keeps the same 12-character prefix), the rule that a different commit, other arguments or another candidate drop the steps but keep the writes, outputs JSON would change ({200: 14}) refused, and a fixed layout shared with the skill's instructions, checked with a file the skill wrote.

Part 3: the fixed publish parameter comes from the lesson's Use It contract (publish: fixed_false). Text is never turned into a boolean, so the bool("false") trap appears once in this pack (Part 1); int() leniency (" 3", "+3") is not tested because lessons 05, 18 and 20 of this chapter already test that kind of trap. The part ends with SkillHost.prepare, which runs Part 1's router before binding.

Part 4: the suggested subagent trap (a subagent gets the skill without the parent's history) moved to Part 5's fork mode so the same thing is not tested twice. The stream adds a denied stage, so refused invocations and tool calls show in the trace, and leaves argument binding to Part 3. Approvals are checked within a turn, across turns and across a compaction; the reload happens before the skill's next tool call, through load_body, and picks up a changed SKILL.md (revision r2).

Part 5: fallback is the value the caller continues with, and None means stop (the Use It contract's missing_dependency: stop); a stop raises inside the caller and is decided by the caller's own request, up to the session's skill. A request's max_depth also bounds every call below it, so a deeper request cannot raise an earlier limit. The host policy's skill caller allowlist is not involved. There is no diamond and no repeated call, because the visited-set-versus-chain trap is already tested twice in this chapter (11 and 23).

Kept apart from neighbouring lessons: no evaluation metrics (27), routing selects skills rather than models (21), Part 5 runs call chains at run time instead of checking static dependency edges (22), and nothing here discovers skills or budgets the catalog (24).
